claims.text: Spin-polarized neutron diffraction can reveal a ferromagnetic ground state.
Long-range ferromagnetic spin alignment will produce distinct polarization-dependent Bragg peaks.
Measurements at different temperatures can help distinguish the relevant magnetic ordering behavior.
Applied-field variation can differentiate intrinsic magnetic order from field-induced effects.
The crystal lattice serves as a scaffold for aligned magnetic domains.
Spin-polarized neutrons interact differently with aligned and disordered magnetic moments.
Uniform spin alignment in a ferromagnetic ground state produces additional magnetic scattering signals.
The magnetic scattering signals vary with neutron polarization.
Polarization-dependent magnetic Bragg peaks unambiguously distinguish ferromagnetic ordering from other magnetic and nonmagnetic states.
A ferromagnetically ordered material will show polarization-dependent magnetic Bragg peaks.
The intensity of magnetic Bragg peaks will change with applied magnetic field.
The intensity of magnetic Bragg peaks will change with temperature.
Unpolarized neutron diffraction does not show polarization-dependent magnetic peaks.
Non-ferromagnetic samples do not show distinct polarization-dependent magnetic peaks.
Instrument sensitivity can limit the method's resolution.
Complex microstructures and overlapping spin-glass or antiferromagnetic contributions can complicate interpretation of the scattering pattern.
Coexisting magnetic phases or small magnetic domains can make the extent of ferromagnetic order difficult to quantify in complex alloys.
Absence of significant polarization-dependent magnetic Bragg peaks rules out a ferromagnetic ground state.
Failure of expected peak intensities to change with field and temperature rules out a ferromagnetic ground state.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says the method unambiguously differentiates ferromagnetism from other states, whereas the boundary and uncertainty fields state that overlapping magnetic orders, coexisting phases, microstructure, and domain size can make interpretation ambiguous.

The falsification rule treats absence of polarization-dependent peaks as decisive evidence against ferromagnetism, but the stated sensitivity and domain-size limitations provide alternative reasons why such peaks might not be detected.
